title: The Sz.-Nagy–Kato intertwiner
subtitle: G2 lecture 048000 · expanded mathematical companion
adaptation: Standalone companion adapted from the source spoken lecture and display-only mathematics appendix. Explicit hypotheses, stepwise proofs, worked examples, and local vector diagrams; no narration edits.

slides.title: Construct transport without choosing bases
slides.lead: Two nearby orthogonal projections determine a canonical operator that carries each side of one decomposition toward the other.
body: Write P and Q for the projections onto U and V. On U, transport by projecting into V; on U⊥, transport by projecting into V⊥. Adding the two pieces creates the Sz.-Nagy–Kato intertwiner K.
The construction is intrinsic to P and Q. Its polar factor removes the stretching and yields a unitary transport when the gap is uniformly below one.
slides.takeaway: Projection blocks produce the transport candidate before any basis is chosen.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 048000 · Construct transport without choosing bases

slides.title: Assemble the two complementary pieces
slides.lead: The canonical candidate acts separately on the source subspace and its orthogonal complement.
body: For x in U, Kx=Qx lies in V. For x in U⊥, Kx=(I−Q)x lies in V⊥. These two outputs are orthogonal, which simplifies every norm calculation.
Unlike an arbitrary map carrying U onto V, K simultaneously respects both complementary decompositions. It is the correct object to normalize with polar decomposition.
slides.takeaway: K sends source and source-complement components to matching target sides.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 048000 · Assemble the two complementary pieces

slides.title: The intertwining identity
slides.lead: The projector algebra shows that K respects the selected subspaces exactly.
body: Multiplying the definition of K by P on the right keeps only QP. Multiplying on the left by Q also keeps only QP. Therefore KP=QK.
The same argument gives K(I−P)=(I−Q)K. Thus once K is normalized to a unitary, its polar factor will carry U to V and U⊥ to V⊥.
slides.takeaway: Intertwining is built into K rather than imposed after the fact.

slides.title: Compute the exact modulus
slides.lead: Orthogonality of K’s two output parts gives a surprising identity.
body: Expand K* K, using P²=P and Q²=Q. Its diagonal blocks are PQP and (I−P)(I−Q)(I−P). Collecting terms yields I−(P−Q)².
This is exactly the square of the positive cosine operator. Hence |K|=C, the same operator that measures cosine of the principal angles.
slides.takeaway: K is cosine-sized transport: its modulus is the positive angle cosine.

slides.title: The one-plane calculation
slides.lead: On a principal plane meeting at angle θ, K is cos θ times the ordinary rotation through θ.
body: If e spans U and f spans U⊥, the target basis is v=cos θ e+sin θ f and v⊥=−sin θ e+cos θ f. Applying K to e and f produces cos θ v and cos θ v⊥.
Therefore K shrinks both principal-plane directions by cos θ while turning them through θ. Its polar normalization removes precisely that shrinkage.
slides.takeaway: The scalar cosine is the stretching that must be removed.

slides.title: A simple invertibility test
slides.lead: The deviation K−I can be factored directly in terms of the projection difference.
body: Expanding K and subtracting I gives (Q−P)(2P−I). Because 2P−I is a reflection, its norm is one; thus ‖K−I‖≤‖Q−P‖.
If d=‖P−Q‖<1, K is invertible by the Neumann-series argument. The same hypothesis gives C≥√(1−d²)I, so the positive modulus also has a bounded inverse.
slides.takeaway: A gap below one makes both K and its positive modulus boundedly invertible.

slides.title: Normalize with polar decomposition
slides.lead: Remove the cosine stretching by multiplying K with the inverse of its positive modulus.
body: Set W=KC^{-1}. Since K*K=C² and C commutes with the source projection P, the result is unitary. Multiplying KP=QK by C^{-1} preserves the intertwining identity.
Hence WP=QW, and W sends U onto V and U⊥ onto V⊥. This is a unitary transport specified entirely by the two projections.
slides.takeaway: Polar normalization turns cosine-sized transport into a unitary intertwiner.

slides.title: Why no arbitrary coordinate choices appear
slides.lead: The operations defining W are addition, multiplication, adjoint, positive square root, and inversion.
body: Every one of these operations is intrinsic to the original operators P and Q. Changing orthonormal coordinates conjugates the whole construction consistently, without changing which geometric map it represents.
This is important when principal angles repeat: an eigenbasis inside a repeated-angle space is not unique, but K and W remain well defined.
slides.takeaway: The transport is canonical under change of coordinates and repeated angles.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 048000 · Why no arbitrary coordinate choices appear

slides.title: Extending beyond uniform gaps
slides.lead: The formula W=KC^{-1} depends on the quantitative condition C≥cI.
body: When the crossed defect spaces vanish but the cosine spectrum approaches zero, C may have no bounded inverse. Nevertheless, K can be injective with dense range.

The polar decomposition K=WC still supplies a unitary W in that acute setting. Working with the polar factor, rather than writing C^{-1}, is what makes the construction extend to the weaker hypothesis.
slides.mathtex: K=WC\quad\text{with }W\text{ unitary when crossed defects vanish}
slides.takeaway: Polar decomposition is more general than literal division by C.

slides.title: Reconstruct the construction
slides.lead: The key identities can be verified directly from P²=P and Q²=Q.
body: Compute KP and QK, then expand K*K. On a tilted two-dimensional plane, calculate K explicitly and identify the factor cos θ. Finally, normalize K and check WP=QW.
This chain of steps shows why the same positive cosine operator appears in principal-angle geometry and in the canonical unitary transport between nearby subspaces.
slides.takeaway: Intertwining plus polar normalization gives direct geometric transport.
